the classification of point sources into quasars, galaxies and stars.
a machine learning approach to classifying objects in SDSS images.
the development of a machine learning algorithm to identify point-like sources in the SDSS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our catalogue contains a large number of quasaries, stars and galaxies, and is a good representation of the SDSS DR7 data set.
the completeness of our catalogue for quasars brighter than i =21.3 and stars to i = 21.7 is better than 99 per cent, and the contamination by stars and galaxies is less than 1 per cent.
our catalogue contains 99.96+/- 0.01 per cent of spectroscopic quasars brighter than i =21.3, and 99.5+/-0.5 per cent of stars brighter than i =21.3 in a colour range of 0.2 < i − r < 2.0.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our catalogue is 99.9 per cent pure for i ∈ [14, 21.3] and 99.9 per cent complete for i ≤ 19.5.

we have produced a catalogue of six million objects in the SDSS that can be used for photometric redshift studies and other applications where a large sample of objects with photometric redshifts is required.
we have created a catalogue that is 99.96 per cent pure and complete to i = 21.3, which is the brightest magnitude that we study.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the photometric classifier presented here is capable of identifying the vast majority of quasars in the SDSS, and can therefore be used to identify new quasars for spectroscopic follow-up.
we provide a simple and fast algorithm for classifying photometric objects in the SDSS.
the photometric classifier is robust enough to be used in the SDSS Data Release 12 (DR12) to select a sample of quasars that will be used for cosmology in future work.
